cards.text: Jesus is in Jerusalem now, and He walks into the temple courts. There are people in there selling. In the TEMPLE, friend.

cards.question: Jesus walks into the temple courts and finds people selling there. What does He do?

answers.text: He begins to drive them out
He asks the priests about it

cards.text: And Jesus doesn't just drive them out. He tells them what's written in Scripture about God's house.

cards.question: God's house is meant to be a house of prayer. What does Jesus tell the sellers they've made it?

cards.text: After that, Jesus is teaching at the temple EVERY day. But the chief priests, the scribes and the leaders of the people are intent on killing Him.

cards.question: The chief priests, scribes and leaders of the people want to kill Jesus. Why can't they find a way to do it?

answers.text: All the people hang on His words
His disciples stand guard around Him

cards.text: One day Jesus is teaching the people in the temple courts and proclaiming the gospel, when up walk the chief priests, the scribes AND the elders. Friend, that's the whole group chat showing up in person.

cards.question: The chief priests, scribes and elders walk up to Jesus in the temple courts. What do they demand to know?

answers.text: By what authority He does these things
Which teacher trained Him in the law
How long He plans to stay in the city

cards.text: Jesus doesn't hand them an answer. He tells them He's got a question for them too.

cards.question: Jesus has a question of His own for the chief priests, scribes and elders. What's it about?

cards.text: That's John the Baptist, who went all around the Jordan preaching a baptism of repentance (Luke 3:3). Jesus asks them whether John's baptism was from heaven or from men.
The leaders huddle up and talk it over among themselves. Like coworkers trying to word a reply to the boss so it doesn't come back on them.

cards.question: The leaders figure that if they say John's baptism was from heaven, Jesus will ask why they didn't believe John.
If the leaders say John's baptism was from men, they'll have trouble with the crowd, because the people are convinced John was a ___.
If the leaders say John's baptism was from men, what do they think the people will do to them?
The leaders have talked it over. What do they finally tell Jesus about John's baptism?
Since the leaders won't say where John's baptism came from, Jesus goes ahead and tells them where His own authority comes from.

cards.text: Jesus replies, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I am doing these things." Two questions asked, friend, and ZERO answers.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "He starts teaching the sellers" is arguably true in the passage. In Luke 19:46 Jesus declares Scripture to the sellers, and in 19:47 He is teaching at the temple every day. A baker could argue this answer is right.

rule.text: Each wrong answer must be false anywhere in the passage, not just at that moment.

findings.problem: The question says the leaders "demand to know." In the text they say "Tell us" and ask a question (Luke 20:2). Calling it a demand gives it a tone the text doesn't name.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The wrong answer "Which teacher trained Him in the law" is close to the second half of the leaders' question, "who gave You this authority?" (Luke 20:2). A baker could argue it matches what they asked.

rule.text: No near-matches. A wrong answer never means the same as the right answer, or close to it. If a baker could argue it's right, replace it.

findings.problem: "Two questions asked, friend, and ZERO answers" says something the text shows isn't true. Luke 20:7 says "they answered that they did not know where it was from." The count is also unclear: the leaders' question in 20:2 has two parts, and Jesus asks one more.

rule.text: Noticing: What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: Papa Dorin's voice is flat across the walkthrough. Only cards 1, 7, 12 and 18 try for humor, and those lines are mild ("In the TEMPLE, friend."). Most story cards, like 3, 5, 9 and 11, read as plain narration. There is no real laugh-out-loud moment, even where the text gives room for one, such as the leaders huddling over a question with no safe answer.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
